questions.stem: Which statement is the full definition of a catalyst?

options.text: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction but is chemically unchanged at the end
options.explanation: Both the speed-up and the unchanged state are required.

options.text: A substance that makes reactions happen that would never occur
options.explanation: Catalysts change pace, not possibility.

options.text: A substance consumed to provide energy for the reaction
options.explanation: Catalysts are not consumed and do not fuel reactions.

options.text: Any substance present in small amounts
options.explanation: Small amount is a feature, not the definition.

questions.stem: Why do small amounts of catalyst suffice?

options.text: Because the catalyst is not consumed and can keep working
options.explanation: Being unchanged at the end means one batch can process far more reactant.

options.text: Because catalysts are too expensive to waste
options.explanation: Cost may be true industrially, but the chemical reason is non-consumption.

options.text: Because a small mass reacts completely
options.explanation: The catalyst does not react away at all.

options.text: Because catalysts dissolve into the products
options.explanation: Dissolving is not part of catalysis here.

questions.stem: Where does the catalyst appear in a chemical equation?

options.text: Above or below the reaction arrow
options.explanation: The arrow position shows the catalyst aids the change without being a reactant.

options.text: On the left with the reactants
options.explanation: That would list it as a reactant, which it is not.

options.text: On the right with the products
options.explanation: It is not produced by the reaction.

options.text: Nowhere, since catalysts are secret
options.explanation: Industrial equations routinely show catalysts over the arrow.

questions.stem: A reaction finishes with 2 g of solid catalyst recovered from 2 g added. What does this show?

options.text: The substance acted as a catalyst, unchanged in mass by the reaction
options.explanation: Matching start and end masses are the expected behaviour of a catalyst.

options.text: The catalyst must have doubled in activity
options.explanation: Mass recovery says nothing about activity doubling.

options.text: The catalyst was the product
options.explanation: Products are made by the reaction; the catalyst was present at the start.

options.text: The reaction never happened
options.explanation: The reaction can proceed fully while the catalyst stays unchanged.

questions.stem: Which is a consequence of using a catalyst in an industrial process?

options.text: A faster production rate without the catalyst being consumed
options.explanation: Speed rises while the catalyst batch keeps working, which is why industry invests in it.

options.text: The products become different chemicals
options.explanation: Catalysts change the pace, not the identity of the products.

options.text: The equation must be rebalanced
options.explanation: Balancing is untouched by catalysis.

options.text: The reaction becomes irreversible
options.explanation: Reversibility is unaffected by adding a catalyst.

questions.stem: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?

options.text: By providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy
options.explanation: The lower hurdle lets more collisions lead to products.

options.text: By heating the reaction mixture
options.explanation: Catalysts are not heaters; temperature is a separate factor.

options.text: By increasing the concentration of reactants
options.explanation: Concentration is untouched by the catalyst.

options.text: By weakening the products so they form sooner
options.explanation: Product strength is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: What happens to the activation energy of the uncatalysed route when a catalyst is added?

options.text: It stays the same; the catalyst opens a new, lower route alongside it
options.explanation: The original pathway still exists; the alternative is simply easier.

options.text: It falls, because the catalyst lowers every barrier
options.explanation: The uncatalysed route is untouched; only the new route is lower.

options.text: It doubles, because two routes now compete
options.explanation: Competition between routes does not raise any barrier.

options.text: It disappears entirely
options.explanation: The catalysed route still has its own, smaller barrier.

questions.stem: Iron in the ammonia process and vanadium(V) oxide in the sulfur process are examples of what?

options.text: Different catalysts chosen for different industrial processes
options.explanation: Each process pairs with a catalyst suited to it, all working on the same principle.

options.text: Reactants consumed by their reactions
options.explanation: Both substances are recovered unchanged after the process.

options.text: Products of their reactions
options.explanation: Neither is a product; both pre-date the reaction.

options.text: Fuels burned to heat the processes
options.explanation: They are not burned; they host the reaction on their surfaces.

questions.stem: Why does a lower-energy pathway raise the reaction rate?

options.text: A greater proportion of collisions now carry enough energy to react
options.explanation: Lowering the hurdle promotes more ordinary collisions into successful ones.

options.text: Because particles collide less often but harder
options.explanation: Frequency does not fall; the success rate rises.

options.text: Because the catalyst collides with the particles
options.explanation: Collisions with the catalyst surface are part of the route, not the rate logic.

options.text: Because the products leave faster
options.explanation: Product departure is not the rate-determining idea here.

questions.stem: Which biological molecules act as catalysts?

options.text: Enzymes
options.explanation: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of living systems on the same lower-pathway principle.

options.text: Fats
options.explanation: Fats store energy; they do not catalyse.

options.text: Sugars
options.explanation: Sugars are respiratory fuels, not catalysts.

options.text: Water molecules
options.explanation: Water is a solvent or reactant here, not the biological catalyst.
